findings.matters: Towns Fund is time-limited government financing for regeneration. Slipping 93% of approved budget in Q1 risks losing grant allocation if delivery deadlines are missed, and signals serious project delivery or planning failures.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring Quarter 1 2026/27
findings.headline: Only 6.89% of revised £126.2m capital programme spent in first quarter, with £58.7m already reprofiled out
findings.detail: Capital expenditure to 30 June was £8.696m representing 6.89% of the revised programme. Combined with £58.7m of major projects already reprofiled into future years (Star Square and Town Deal), this low Q1 spend rate raises questions about the council's ability to execute its capital programme as planned.
findings.matters: Slow Q1 spend combined with substantial project reprofiling indicates potential constraints on the council's project delivery capacity. For a lender, this affects confidence in cashflow forecasting, the council's ability to realise strategic investments, and future capital financing needs.
findings.figures: £8.696m spent of £126.2m revised programme (6.89%); £58.7m reprofiled (Star Square £34.339m + Town Deal £24.362m)

findings.paper_title: EB Corporate Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/27 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Reserves and Balances eroding from £102.896m at start of year to forecast £89.949m, with General Reserve at £6m
findings.detail: The council started 2026/27 with £102.896m in reserves and balances. By end of Q1, forecast position is £89.949m — a reduction of £12.947m (£8.880m planned drawdown plus £1.982m additional due to overspend). The General Reserve is held at £6m. Repeated reserve draws reduce the council's ability to absorb volatility or unexpected costs.
findings.matters: Declining reserves indicate constrained financial resilience. If overspends continue, the General Reserve of £6m may come under pressure, limiting flexibility for one-off costs or service disruptions.
findings.figures: Starting reserves: £102.896m; forecast ending: £89.949m; General Reserve: £6.000m; Schools Balances: £8.341m

findings.paper_title: EB Corporate Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/27 Quarter 1
findings.headline: High Needs DSG deficit forecast at £16.905m, dependent on government grant approval and Statutory Override expiry in March 2028
findings.detail: The High Needs DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) holds a £16.905m deficit forecast for 2026/27. The council has applied for a High Needs Stability Grant of c£4.585m to cover 90% of brought-forward deficit if its SEND Reform Plan is approved by the Department for Education. The residual deficit must be funded from the General Fund when the Statutory Override expires in March 2028. This is a known structural issue but creates a future obligation.
findings.matters: This represents a material liability for General Fund reserves from 2028 onwards, even with government grant. It constrains long-term financial flexibility and depends on government policy decisions.
findings.figures: £16.905m forecast DSG deficit; £5.094m deficit brought forward from 2025/26; c£4.585m grant expected if approved; Statutory Override expires March 2028

Once our SEND reform plans are approved and we receive the £4.585m grant to cover 90% of the brought forward deficit, we are hoping the government will follow the same approach for tackling deficits in FY 2026/27 and 2027/28.

This reduces financial flexibility mid-year.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns reduce the council's buffer to absorb future shocks or volatility. A growing overspend in Q1 signals cash flow pressures and potential full-year deterioration.
findings.figures: £1.982m forecast overspend; £8.880m already planned reserve drawdown; forecast additional £1.982m drawdown required

findings.paper_title: EB Corporate Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/27 Quarter 1
findings.headline: SEN Transport overspend of £3.173m is the main driver of the Children portfolio's £1.008m overspend
findings.detail: The council forecasts a £3.173m overspend on SEN Transport due to continuing increasing demand and higher costs, which is explicitly noted as a growing pressure. This is partly offset by underspends in other Children services, but the net effect is a £1.008m portfolio overspend. The issue is demand-driven and structural.
findings.matters: Demand-led overspends in SEND are notoriously difficult to control and often predict future years' deficits. This is a material cost that will likely persist and grow.

findings.paper_title: EB Corporate Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Investment balance of £93.7M includes advance receipt of capital grants (Darwen Town Deal, Levelling Up) due for future spend.
findings.detail: The council's unusually high investment balance (£93.7M at year-end, ranging £94M–£139M during year) is explicitly driven by timing of grant receipts received in advance of project expenditure. These include Darwen Town Deal and Levelling Up funding. These balances represent committed future spend that will draw down the council's liquidity as capital projects progress.
findings.matters: Advance grant receipts create a cash dependency: the council holds other parties' money and must deliver schemes as planned. Delivery delays create timing pressures and potential clawback risk; successful delivery creates cash outflows that tighten liquidity at a time when the council also faces a growing borrowing requirement.
findings.figures: Total investments £93.7M at 31 March 2026; investment balance range £94M–£139M during year
findings.quote: Investment balances have remained high during this year, largely due to the timing of funds received from central government and significant capital grants received in advance of spend being incurred, including Darwen Town Deal and Levelling Up funding.

findings.paper_title: EB Corporate Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Net borrowing requirement forecast to grow from £14.6M to £141.5M over three years as council depletes reserves to fund capital programmes.
findings.detail: The liability benchmark forecast shows the council's net loans requirement growing substantially from £14.6M (actual, 31 March 2026) to £94.4M (2027), £136.8M (2028), and £141.5M (2029). This reflects a structural gap between capital financing need and available reserves. The council's existing borrowing of £108.3M is currently above the minimum risk benchmark of £24.6M; the forecast shows borrowing will need to grow materially as reserves are deployed.
findings.matters: This shows a material structural shift from internal borrowing to external borrowing over the medium term. A lender needs clarity on timing of new borrowing, availability of sources (PWLB, markets), and whether the council's revenue position can support the resulting debt service and interest costs.
findings.quote: The liability benchmark is an important tool to help establish whether the Council is likely to be a long-term borrower or long-term investor in the future and so shape its strategic focus and decision making.

findings.paper_title: EB Corporate Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital expenditure delivered at only 35% of budget: £49.6M actual against £143.1M planned.
findings.detail: The council spent only £49.6M of its planned £143.1M capital budget in 2025/26, a £93.5M or 65% underspend. The capital financing requirement also came in significantly below estimate (£286.9M actual vs £351.0M estimated). The report does not explain the variance. This suggests either unrealistic planning or delivery constraints affecting the council's ability to execute capital schemes.
findings.matters: Large capital programme variances indicate planning or execution risk. For a lender, this raises questions about the council's ability to deliver its regeneration strategy and the reliability of its financial forecasting and project management.
findings.figures: £49.6M outturn vs £143.1M budget (65% underspend); Capital Financing Requirement £286.9M actual vs £351.0M estimated
findings.quote: Outturn capital spend was £49.6M, which is below the £143.1M anticipated at the start of the year.

findings.paper_title: EB Corporate Capital Budget and Balance Sheet 2025/26 – Outturn
findings.headline: £60.132m of capital budget slipped to future years, including £30.153m on Blackburn Town Centre Business Innovation Phase 1
findings.detail: The capital programme decreased from £98.810m to £49.565m largely due to £60.132m of slippage into future years. The Blackburn Town Centre project alone accounts for £30.153m of this, re-profiled across 2026-2030. While some slippage is routine, this scale raises questions about delivery capacity or financing certainty.
findings.matters: Large capital programme slippage, particularly on a single £44.135m regeneration project, can indicate either funding constraints or project delivery challenges. A lender would want assurance that the reprofiled spending is properly funded and deliverable.
findings.figures: Total capital slippage: £60.132m; Blackburn Town Centre Business Innovation Phase 1: £44.135m total budget with £30.153m re-profiled to 2026-2030; original budget approved February 2026 was £98.810m, outturn £49.565m

This budget will subsequently be carried forward to be used in 2026/27 (as part of the total of £30.153 million included in the slippage table below). The remaining budget of £44.135 million (£2.647 million of which was spent in 2025/26) has been reprofiled to reflect the overall forecast expenditure from 2026 to 2030.

findings.paper_title: EB Corporate Capital Budget and Balance Sheet 2025/26 – Outturn
findings.headline: Council tax arrears increased by £765k year-on-year despite marginally improved collection rate
findings.detail: Council tax arrears rose from £14.058m to £14.823m (5.4% increase), a material absolute increase even though the collection rate improved from 95.2% to 95.3%. The improvement in collection rate is outweighed by the rising arrears stock, suggesting growing resident payment difficulties.
findings.matters: Rising council tax arrears indicate stress in residents' ability to pay rates. This is a leading indicator of economic deterioration in the area and predictive of future collection problems.

findings.detail: Business rates arrears rose from £1.217m to £1.594m (a £377k increase year-on-year), and the collection rate fell by one percentage point. This dual deterioration is concerning: both the absolute amount owed and the percentage of rates collected are moving in the wrong direction simultaneously.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates signal economic stress among business ratepayers and represent material loss of reliable income. This trend could accelerate if local economic conditions deteriorate further.

findings.paper_title: EB Corporate Revenue Budget 2025/26 – Outturn
findings.headline: Legal Services overspent by £622k due to additional unbudgeted childcare legal fees, suggesting higher volume or complexity of looked after children cases.
findings.detail: The Finance and Governance portfolio showed an overall underspend of £378k, but this masked a significant overspend in Legal Services of £622k. The report specifically attributes this to 'additional unbudgeted Childcare Legal Fees' (£77k identified separately), along with costs in Legal Services Practice relating to salary and supplies, and underachievement on court costs recovered. This appears directly related to the elevated number of looked after children proceedings.
findings.matters: Childcare legal fees are a secondary cost associated with the LAC pressures already identified. Higher than expected legal spend signals not just higher LAC numbers but potentially greater complexity of cases, which correlates with more expensive placements and ongoing service pressures.
findings.figures: £622k overspend on Legal Services; £77k specifically on Childcare Legal Fees
findings.quote: the overspend on Legal Services of £622k is due to additional unbudgeted Childcare Legal Fees, £77k on Legal Services Practice relating to salary and supplies and service costs, and underachievement on court costs recovered

findings.paper_title: EB Corporate Revenue Budget 2025/26 – Outturn
findings.headline: High Needs DSG (Special Educational Needs funding) created a £5.094m cumulative deficit, currently protected by Statutory Override until March 2028 but dependent on government grant approval to avoid funding the gap from General Fund reserves.
findings.detail: The High Needs block overspent by £7.180m in 2025/26. The council experienced a 25% increase in independent special school placements (105 budgeted to 131 placed) and a 6% increase in the cost of EHCPs in mainstream schools (adding £0.986m). The £6.781m drawn from reserves left a DSG deficit of £5.094m. Although protected by Statutory Override until March 2028, the council is relying on a High Needs Stability Grant of c£4.585m (subject to DfE approval of their SEND Reform Plan) to cover most of the deficit. Any shortfall must be met from General Fund when the override expires.
findings.matters: SEND cost escalation is a national crisis and largely outside council control. The Statutory Override is temporary shelter. If the government grant is not approved, if it is lower than expected, or if SEND demand continues to escalate, the council will face a forced drawdown of approximately £0.5m from General Fund in 2028, plus any additional pressures accumulated by then.
findings.figures: £7.180m overspend in 2025/26; £5.094m cumulative DSG deficit; £4.585m expected grant (subject to approval); independent special school placements up 25% (105 to 131); EHCPs in mainstream schools up 6% = £0.986m
findings.quote: The Council experienced an increase of 25% in the need to place children in independent special schools (105 budgeted to 131 placed), this was on top of the 5% of additional special school places we created for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: EB Corporate Revenue Budget 2025/26 – Outturn
findings.headline: Children's Services overspent by £8.518m, driven primarily by a £9.517m overspend on looked after children in residential and independent fostering placements.
findings.detail: The council's looked-after children service overspent substantially due to both rising numbers of placements and escalating costs. A secondary pressure of £1.814m came from SEN Transport, driven by increasing numbers of children eligible for home-to-school transport with EHCPs. The council underspent in other service areas (Leaving Care, Education, Early Years) but these only partially offset the main pressures.
findings.matters: Looked after children and SEND transport are demand-driven, escalating costs that are difficult to control through normal workforce or budget management. If these trends continue or accelerate, they represent a structural deficit that will require either significant service redesign, external funding solutions, or sustained reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: £8.518m total portfolio overspend; £9.517m on looked after children placements; £1.814m on SEN Transport
findings.quote: Rising numbers of children placed in expensive residential and independent fostering placements, alongside rising costs, saw this budget overspend by £9.517m.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 9 - Annual Risk Management Report 2025.2026
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creating distraction from core governance and financial management
findings.detail: Two new risks (38 and 39) identify that Lancashire Combined County Authority's uncertain progression to a mayoral model, combined with simultaneous LGR, is consuming council management capacity. Risk 39 specifically warns the council cannot adequately support both the LCCA transition and LGR response simultaneously.
findings.matters: Governance disruption during major structural change creates risk that financial controls, audit functions, and service oversight will weaken. Major reorganisations have historically caused councils to miss deadlines and commitments.
findings.figures: None; described as capacity/distraction risk
findings.quote: Risk 39: The risks associated with potential lack of capacity within the Council from continuing to provide support to the LCCA and its on-going development whilst responding to and managing Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) and the distraction that these two areas may create for the Council.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 9 - Annual Risk Management Report 2025.2026
findings.headline: Equal pay audit revealed job role valuation gaps requiring remediation
findings.detail: Risk 40 (new) identifies that jobs have not been formally re-evaluated for equal pay purposes at required intervals. First equal pay audit has been completed and progress made, but risk remains that claims could be successful if roles have been undervalued relative to comparable roles.
findings.matters: Equal pay claims in local government have exposed councils to very large settlements. Failure to maintain up-to-date job valuations is a documented gap that increases litigation risk.
findings.figures: None given; described as having made progress
findings.quote: Risk 40: The failure to re-evaluate jobs roles at least every five years to ensure an up to date rank order of jobs and objectively apply HR policies and processes relating to pay and terms and conditions could lead to a successful equal pay claim.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 9 - Annual Risk Management Report 2025.2026
findings.headline: Municipal Mutual Insurance scheme exposes council to £2.3m contingent liability
findings.detail: The council is liable under the MMI scheme of arrangement for legacy claims from historical cover pre-1992. Currently self-insuring 25% of claims (£494,000 paid since 2014). Estimated potential exposure is £2.3m, though further levies could increase this over 10–20 years as historical occupational disease claims emerge.
findings.matters: This is a known but uncertain liability, quantified by the council as potentially material, included in contingent liabilities and affecting minimum reserves policy. Lenders need to understand tail risks like this.
findings.figures: £494,000 already paid since 2014; £315,000 provision; estimated total exposure £2.3m at current calculation; currently 25% self-insured (75% scheme's responsibility)
findings.quote: the Council previously estimated the potential cost to the Council, if the scheme is invoked, could be over £2.3 million at the current calculation, along with any new claims. This is taken into account when the minimum level of balances is reviewed during the annual budget process

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 9 - Annual Risk Management Report 2025.2026
findings.headline: Tree safety incident resulted in a fatality
findings.detail: During 2025/26 a large tree branch fell in Witton Park resulting in a death. This incident triggered tree management (Risk 41) becoming a top strategic risk and illustrates real operational exposure beyond abstract risk registers.
findings.matters: Fatality increases reputational risk, potential litigation, and demonstrates inadequacy of prior asset management. Councils can face claims for negligent tree management. The council must now invest to prevent recurrence.
findings.figures: One fatality recorded
findings.quote: Several fallen tree incidents at locations including East Park Road, The Crescent at Cherry tree, Woodgates Road, Meins Road, Sunnyhurst Woods and a large branch falling in Witton Park that resulted in a fatality.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 9 - Annual Risk Management Report 2025.2026
findings.headline: Adult social care at risk from NHS integrated care board's budget deficit
findings.detail: Listed as the council's top risk (Risk 33), negative impact on care services could flow from Lancashire & South Cumbria ICB's 2023/24 budget deficit and future savings plans. These decisions are beyond the council's control but directly affect what the council must fund.
findings.matters: Adult social care is typically a significant council budget (often 40%+ of net spend). An NHS funding gap could force the council to either cut services, increase council tax, or use reserves.

findings.headline: Public liability claims jumped 225% to £2m in one year
findings.detail: Total public liability claim values increased from £629,601 in 2024/25 to £2,048,460 in 2025/26. Whilst the number of claims fell (119 to 94), individual claims appear to be significantly larger. The council must provision for these or carry additional exposure.
findings.matters: A £1.4m swing in liability claims in one year represents material unplanned cost requiring reserves or insurance provisions; lenders assess reserve adequacy when deciding lending capacity
findings.quote: Total Potential Value of Claims... Public Liability... 2024/25 £629,601  2025/26 £2,048,460

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 12 - Annual Governance Statement 2025 26
findings.headline: Council faces abolition due to local government reorganisation with expected end date of March 2028, creating strategic uncertainty
findings.detail: The Council's Corporate Plan has been extended to March 2028 to align with the 'expected abolition date of the Council due to local government reorganisation.' This means the Council is operating under a clear end-date of service, which affects medium-term planning and may impact service continuity and financial sustainability planning.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council's operating model and financial position will be affected by reorganisation, creating uncertainty around debt repayment timelines and potential changes to funding arrangements
findings.figures: Expected abolition date: March 2028
findings.quote: Members affirmed the Corporate Missions at Policy Council in December 2025. At this meeting the Council also agreed to extend the current corporate plan to 2028. This aligns with the expected abolition date of the Council due to local government reorganisation.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 12 - Annual Governance Statement 2025 26
findings.headline: Council lacks agreed project management methodology across the organisation, creating governance gap
findings.detail: The statement explicitly notes that 'The Council does not currently have an agreed methodology in place for managing projects and programmes of work across the Council.' Work is underway to develop and implement a corporate approach with agreed principles, processes and tools.
findings.matters: Absence of consistent project management standards increases risk of cost overruns, missed deadlines, and poor governance of major transformation programmes that may be central to achieving the Council's savings targets
findings.figures: No agreed methodology currently in place
findings.quote: The Council does not currently have an agreed methodology in place for managing projects and programmes of work across the Council.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 12 - Annual Governance Statement 2025 26
findings.headline: Increasing data breaches and Information Commissioner complaints, with 100% rise in ICO complaints year-on-year
findings.detail: The total number of data breaches recorded for 2025/26 was 116, a 0.9% increase on the previous year (115). Complaints to the Information Commissioner's Office rose from 3 in 2024/25 to 6 in 2025/26, a 100% increase, though none required further action from the Council.
findings.matters: Rising ICO complaints and data breaches suggest possible weaknesses in information governance and operational controls, with reputational risk if breaches escalate
findings.figures: 116 total data breaches (up 0.9%); 6 ICO complaints (up from 3, 100% increase)
findings.quote: The total number of data breaches recorded for 2025/26 was 116. This is an increase of 0.9% against the previous year (115). 6 complaints made to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). This is a 100% increase on the number of complaints registered with the ICO in 2024/25 (3).

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 12 - Annual Governance Statement 2025 26
findings.headline: External auditor issued disclaimer of opinion on 2024/25 accounts, unable to complete sufficient audit procedures by deadline
findings.detail: The External Auditor could not complete sufficient work to support an audit opinion for the 2024/25 Financial Statements by the statutory deadline and issued a disclaimed opinion in February 2026. However, the auditor noted that work completed did not identify significant weaknesses in financial sustainability, governance, or resource efficiency arrangements.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion, even without identified weaknesses, signals uncertainty over financial reporting assurance and creates compliance risk for both the council and its lenders
findings.figures: 2024/25 audit; disclaimed opinion issued February 2026
findings.quote: The reports set out the reasons that it had not been possible for the Auditor to complete sufficient work to support an audit opinion for the audit of the 2024/25 Financial Statements by the statutory deadline. Therefore, a disclaimer of audit opinion was issued.

findings.paper_title: Agenda Item 12 - Annual Governance Statement 2025 26
findings.headline: Medium-term budget deficit of £5.6m by 2028/29 with current-year overspend already at £6.7m
findings.detail: The Council's Q3 2025/26 forecast outturn showed a £6.7m overspend. The updated Medium Term Financial Plan for 2026/29 indicates a funding gap of £3.8m in 2027/28, rising to £5.6m in 2028/29. The 2026/27 budget, while technically balanced, still requires £4.5m of savings to be achieved across portfolios.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can close growing deficits through deliverable savings or whether reserves will be drawn down unsustainably
findings.figures: £6.7m Q3 2025/26 overspend; £3.8m deficit 2027/28; £5.6m deficit 2028/29; £4.5m savings required in 2026/27
findings.quote: The latest forecast outturn for 2025/26, as set out in the Quarter 3 forecast outturn presented to Executive Board in February 2026, indicated a forecast overspend of £6.7m. Alongside the Revenue Budget for 2026/27, an updated Medium Term Financial Plan 2026/29 was provided which indicated a funding gap of £3.8m in 2027/28, rising to £5.6m in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: BWD Council - Audit Progress Report June 2026
findings.headline: Rebuilding audit assurance over two years to restore unqualified opinion
findings.detail: Forvis Mazars has begun complex risk assessment work to rebuild assurance. They completed some procedures on 2024/25 to support the rebuilding approach. Planning for 2025/26 will commence in July 2026, with the strategy memo to follow. The auditor states the primary focus is supporting the council to return to an unqualified audit report within 2 years.
findings.matters: The timeline matters to creditors. A return to unqualified opinions within 2 years (by 2027/28) signals the audit recovery is progressing, but remains in progress. Until full assurance is restored, financial reporting risk persists.
findings.figures: Two-year timeline to unqualified audit report
findings.quote: The primary focus of our 2025/26 audit will support the Council returning to an unqualified audit report within 2 years.

findings.paper_title: BWD Council - Audit Progress Report June 2026
findings.headline: Three consecutive years of disclaimer opinions on financial statements
findings.detail: Grant Thornton issued a disclaimer for 2022/23 in December 2024. Forvis Mazars then issued disclaimers for both 2023/24 (February 2025) and 2024/25 (February 2026). This means the council's financial statements have not had audit assurance for three years running. The chain started because delays in the 2021/22 audit meant 2022/23 could not be completed by its backstop date, which then left 2023/24's opening balances unaudited and insufficient time to complete 2023/24 within its backstop deadline.
findings.matters: Multiple consecutive disclaimer opinions represent a fundamental governance weakness—creditors and finance directors cannot rely on independently verified financial statements. This raises material questions about the accuracy and reliability of the council's accounts and its financial position.
findings.figures: Three consecutive years: 2022/23 (December 2024), 2023/24 (February 2025), 2024/25 (February 2026)
findings.quote: They issued a Disclaimer of Opinion in their Audit Report on 2 December 2024... We issued a Disclaimer of Opinion on 25th February 2025... We issued a Disclaimer of Opinion on 24th February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Update to the Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/30 and Development of the Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Proposed 3.3% pay award not yet accepted but would add £428k cost pressure in 2027/28
findings.detail: The council budgeted 3.0% for 2026/27 pay. The Employers' pay offer of 3.3% on all pay points SCP2-SCP43 was made March 2026 but not yet accepted by trade unions. Acceptance would add £428k cost pressure in 2027/28, which has been reflected in the current MTFP. This demonstrates ongoing pay negotiations and unresolved cost pressures beyond base budget assumptions.
findings.matters: Known downside risk to budget forecasts; unresolved negotiations could result in additional cost pressures if higher awards are secured
findings.figures: Budgeted pay award 3.0% (2026/27); proposed offer 3.3%; potential additional cost £428k in 2027/28
findings.quote: This has not yet been accepted but would add a cost pressure of £428k in 2027/28

findings.paper_title: Update to the Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/30 and Development of the Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Major capital projects (Darwen Town Deal, King George's Hall, Skills Centre, M65 J5) face price inflation and delivery risks
findings.detail: The council is undertaking significant capital projects with both 'price and delivery risks that may lead to additional funding requirements.' Price inflation on capital costs is rendering some schemes 'undeliverable within the funding envelopes that have been set.' The report notes this may necessitate 'value engineering on projects, identification of additional funds and/or increasing the pace of asset disposals,' as additional borrowing would 'only serve to increase the funding deficit.'
findings.matters: Capital overruns or inability to deliver would require cuts to revenue services or accelerated asset disposals, further pressuring the structural revenue deficit
findings.figures: No specific project overrun amounts identified; multiple major projects flagged as at-risk
findings.quote: price inflation on capital costs rendering some schemes undeliverable within the funding envelopes that have been set

findings.paper_title: Update to the Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/30 and Development of the Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Homelessness costs rising as budget pressure with limited council control
findings.detail: The council identifies homelessness as a key budget delivery risk. While costs are partly masked by Housing Benefit and Supported/Exempt Accommodation, 'the cost of dealing with the homelessness through the use of temporary accommodation has been becoming increasingly prominent in the Council's budget.' The report acknowledges this is 'a pressure being felt by Councils nationally' and that despite innovative service delivery, 'it still remains a risk to the Council.'
findings.matters: Demand-led cost that is growing and largely outside council's direct control, creating structural budget flexibility problem
findings.figures: No specific budget figure provided; identified as ongoing budget risk for 2026/27 and beyond
findings.quote: the cost of dealing with the homelessness through the use of temporary accommodation has been becoming increasingly prominent in the Council's budget

findings.paper_title: Update to the Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/30 and Development of the Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Integrated Care Board financial pressures causing 'cost shunting' to council budgets
findings.detail: The council identifies that the Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB, one of the most financially challenged NHS systems, has created 'instances of cost shunting becoming more frequent.' The ICB faces £36m national cost reduction targets. Council officers note that decisions made by the ICB 'have impacted adversely on the Council's budget (and indeed the budgets of other upper tier authorities).' This represents external cost pressures over which the council has limited control.
findings.matters: Health system financial pressures are being transferred to local authority budgets, creating unplanned and uncontrollable cost pressures beyond council's management
findings.figures: National ICB operating cost reduction target £36m; LA Better Care Grant falls from £10.3m (2026/27) to £0 (2027/28 onwards)
findings.quote: instances of 'cost shunting' becoming more frequent

findings.paper_title: Update to the Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/30 and Development of the Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Adult Social Care commissioning costs (£45m annually) exposed to 6.75% Real Living Wage inflation pressure
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is commissioned at approximately £45m annually, with wages representing around 70% of provider costs. The Real Living Wage increased 6.75% for 2026/27 to £13.45 per hour. The council notes 'the change in National Living Wage has a significant impact on their operating costs' and acknowledges 'above inflation increases in the unit costs over recent years' across both Adults and Children's Social Care driven by provider cost pressures.
findings.matters: Major service budget (£45m) faces cost pressures from wage inflation over which the council has limited control, likely contributing to ongoing deficits and absorbing efficiency gains
findings.figures: Adult Social Care commissioning c£45m annually; wages c70% of provider costs; Real Living Wage increase 6.75% to £13.45/hour
findings.quote: the change in National Living Wage has a significant impact on their operating costs

findings.paper_title: Update to the Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/30 and Development of the Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Council using finite reserves and non-recurring income to balance 2027/28 budget, indicating structural deficit
findings.detail: The 2027/28 budget strategy proposes £1.7m from Budget Support Reserve plus £1.5m from debt recovery/collection fund to close the £4.2m gap, alongside only £1m permanent savings. The report explicitly acknowledges this approach is unsustainable, stating reserves should not be relied upon to support the budget beyond the clear strategy to achieve sustainability. The Budget Support Reserve established to smooth budget cuts will continue depletion.
findings.matters: Using one-off measures to balance recurring deficits cannot continue; indicates council cannot close gap through sustainable service or income changes
findings.figures: 2027/28 funding gap £4.2m; proposed savings £1m; proposed reserve use £1.7m; debt recovery £1.5m
findings.quote: reserves are a finite source of funding and should not be relied upon to support the Council's budget other than as part of the clear strategy to achieve a sustainable budget

findings.paper_title: Update to the Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/30 and Development of the Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: High Needs DSG cumulative deficit forecast at £33m when Statutory Override expires March 2028
findings.detail: The council's DSG reserve went into deficit for the first time at 31 March 2026 (£5.1m). The cumulative deficit is forecast to reach £33.2m by 31 March 2028 when the Statutory Override allowing councils to hold deficits separately expires. Government High Needs Stability Grant should cover 90% (c£4.6m), but the council must fund the residual 10%, potentially c£3.3m. This represents a material unfunded liability that hits the General Fund in 2028/29 unless Government intervention continues.
findings.matters: Major hidden deficit will crystallise in 2028/29 and must be resolved from General Fund, adding to the already-identified structural deficit
findings.figures: DSG deficit at 31/3/26 £5.093m; forecast cumulative by 31/3/28 £33.211m; Council's potential liability c£3.3m; High Needs Stability Grant expected c£4.584m
findings.quote: the cumulative deficit by the time the Statutory Override expires in March 2028 is forecast to be c£33m

findings.paper_title: Update to the Medium Term Financial Plan 2027/30 and Development of the Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Structural funding gap of £9.2m by 2029/30 with no sustainable path to balance
findings.detail: The council's updated MTFP forecasts cumulative funding gaps totalling £9.2m over 2027/30, comprising £4.2m (2027/28), £6.2m (2028/29), and £9.1m (2029/30). The 2027/28 budget strategy proposes only £1m of permanent savings, with the remaining gap addressed through £1.5m debt recovery and £1.7m reserve use. The council explicitly states the objective of achieving a sustainable budget remains unfulfilled.
findings.matters: Indicates structural deficit between recurring spending and revenue funding, requiring sustained service reductions or efficiency programmes unsupported by current proposals
findings.figures: Cumulative gap £9.2m over 2027/30; Gap 2027/28 £4.2m; Proposed savings only £1m; Reserve use £1.7m
findings.quote: the forecast funding gap for the period to 2029/30 is now estimated to be £9.2m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- EB Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council forecast to shift from net investor to net borrower by 2026/27, requiring £60m of additional borrowing by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council currently has more investments than borrowing (net investor position of £90.5m at 31.3.25), but this is forecast to reverse. By 2026/27 the council will require net new borrowing of £3m, rising to £60m by 2028/29. The paper explicitly states the council expects to be a long-term borrower and will use internal resources only as a temporary measure while waiting for interest rates to fall.
findings.matters: This signals the council will return to borrowing markets with significant borrowing needs. Lenders need to know when and how much the council will borrow, and what the council's debt servicing capacity will be.
findings.quote: As demonstrated by the liability benchmark above, the Authority expects to be a long-term borrower but is likely to use internal resources to defer borrowing for as long as possible in the expectation of interest rate reductions by the end of 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- EB Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Usable reserves forecast to decline by 38% over two years, from £150.9m to £92.8m
findings.detail: The council is depleting its reserve position to fund capital spending whilst deferring external borrowing due to high interest rates. Usable reserves fall from £150.9m at 31.3.25 to £127.8m by 31.3.26 and £92.8m by 31.3.27. The strategy relies on grant funding received in advance and capital receipts to sustain this, but the reserves are expected to stabilise only at £77.8m from 2028/29 onwards.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's buffer against financial shocks and signal that the council will have less flexibility to manage unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls without borrowing.
findings.figures: Usable reserves: £150.9m (31.3.25 actual), £127.8m (31.3.26 estimate), £92.8m (31.3.27 forecast), £77.8m (31.3.28-29 forecast)
findings.quote: Table 2: Balance Sheet Summary and Forecast shows Less: Usable reserves (150.9) (127.8) (92.8) (77.8) (77.8) across the forecast period.

findings.paper_title: Blackburn with Darwen Borough Council - Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation introduces strategic uncertainty with five competing structural proposals for Lancashire pending Government decision
findings.detail: In February 2025, the council was invited to develop reorganisation proposals alongside other Lancashire councils. Five different options emerged (ranging from 2-unitary to 5-council structures) by November 2025. Government formal public consultation on its preferred option is expected 'later in 2026'. The outcome could fundamentally change the council's structure, governance, and service delivery model.
findings.matters: Reorganisation creates material uncertainty about the council's future financial capacity and operational viability. Transition costs, potential mergers, and loss of financial independence all represent material risks to lenders with medium-term loans.
findings.figures: 5 proposals submitted by end November 2025; public consultation expected H2 2026; decision timeline undefined
findings.quote: A total of 5 proposals have emerged from the process and are expected to submitted to Government for consideration at the end of November 2025. These proposals are for 2 unitary authorities, 3 such councils, two alternatives for structures of 4 new unitary bodies and finally a 5 council structure for Lancashire. Formal public consultation on the Government's preferred option will begin in later in 2026.

findings.paper_title: Blackburn with Darwen Borough Council - Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Auditors identified £2.2m in unadjusted material misstatements that management did not correct in final accounts
findings.detail: During audit testing, misstatements totalling approximately £2.2m were identified but not corrected by management: £1,265k PPE valuation error (obsolescence factor), £394k asset understatement (fees), and £500k debtor impairment extrapolation. These remain unresolved in the published financial statements.
findings.matters: Unadjusted misstatements of this scale indicate either inadequate controls over financial reporting or management acceptance of material errors. Both scenarios signal elevated risk to financial statement reliability.
findings.figures: Total unadjusted misstatements £2,159k (£1,265k + £394k + £500k)
findings.quote: Dr: Property, Plant and Equipment Cr: Unusable Reserves – Revaluation Reserve Being the value of the higher Obsolescence factor applied incorrectly in a key sample item of our assets tested in our valuations sample testing. 1,265,000 ... Dr: Property, Plant and Equipment Cr: Unusable Reserves – Revaluation Reserve Being the value of understatement of assets identified during sample testing in respect of fees not included in error in the asset valuations. 394,000

findings.paper_title: Blackburn with Darwen Borough Council - Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Eight of 43 completed internal audits received limited assurance ratings due to significant control weaknesses
findings.detail: Limited assurance ratings (indicating significant control weaknesses or errors) were issued on 8 audit assignments. While auditors state these were not considered to have 'significant impact on the overall control environment', the prevalence of control findings (19% of completed audits) indicates systematic weaknesses requiring corrective action.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses increase the risk of undetected financial errors or fraud. This pattern suggests the council's internal control framework may not be operating effectively across multiple business processes.
findings.figures: 8 limited assurance ratings from 43 completed audits (43 of 60 planned completed); 91% of priority 1 audits completed
findings.quote: Eight audits were given a limited assurance rating because significant control weaknesses or other errors were identified. There were no audits undertaken where a rating of no assurance was given although there were a small number receiving an overall limited assurance opinion. These were not considered to have a significant impact on the overall control environment in place within the Council.

findings.paper_title: Blackburn with Darwen Borough Council - Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Projected structural funding gaps of £18.9m (2026/27), £23.2m (2027/28), and £27.0m (2028/29) with plans relying on unspecified savings
findings.detail: The October 2025 Medium Term Financial Plan forecasts three consecutive years of significant funding gaps. The council states these will be addressed through 'service initiatives, savings and the use of reserves' but provides no detailed savings programme. Q3 2025/26 already shows the need to draw an additional £6.6m from reserves in the current year alone.
findings.matters: Multi-year structural deficits of this magnitude indicate the council cannot balance budgets from revenue alone. Lenders assess whether deficits can be closed through identified savings; vague references to 'service initiatives' without detail suggest savings plans are not yet developed.
findings.quote: The Quarter 3 projections for 2025/26 anticipate the Council will be required to use of additional £6.6m from reserves to meet the pressures of overspends emerging through the first half of the year and assuming spend continues for the next six months at the projected rates and without mitigations. The most recent MTFP update (October 2025) therefore projects a funding gap of £18.9m in 2026/27, £23.2m by 2027/28 and £27.0m by 2028/29. These gaps are expected to be funded through a combination of service initiatives, savings and the use of reserves.

findings.paper_title: Blackburn with Darwen Borough Council - Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: High Needs Block (SEND) deficit forecast to reach £15.1m by March 2028, consuming reserves or requiring service cuts
findings.detail: A new SEND deficit of £6.6m emerged in 2025/26. After using £1.6m of reserves, the cumulative deficit stands at £4.9m. Quarter 2 2025-26 forecasts indicate this could grow to £15.1m by March 2028 unless the council receives additional Government funding or cuts SEND spending. The council relies on a statutory override allowing carry-forward only until March 2028; if this is not extended, the full deficit becomes immediately payable.
findings.matters: A £15m unfunded liability represents a material structural deficit driven by rising demand for SEND services. This will force either service reductions, additional borrowing, or significant reserve depletion with no clear resolution strategy.
findings.figures: 2025/26 deficit £6.6m; cumulative after reserves £4.9m; forecast March 2028 £15.1m
findings.quote: The High Needs element for 2025/26 is estimated to have a deficit in year of £6.6m. After using reserves of £1.6m, the cumulative deficit is forecast at £4.9m. This is expected to increase because of the expected demand for additional services for children and young people. The latest forecast of the position, done at Quarter 2 in 2025-26, indicates the deficit could increase to £15.1m by the end of March 2028 unless the Council receives additional funding or can reduce expenditure or demand for SEND services.

findings.paper_title: Blackburn with Darwen Borough Council - Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Auditors issued disclaimer of opinion on financial statements; unable to complete audit procedures before statutory deadline
findings.detail: The auditors could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence before the statutory publication deadline and therefore issued a disclaimer of opinion rather than expressing a standard audit opinion. This means no assurance was provided on whether the financial statements are free from material error. The council published its accounts on 30 June 2025, leaving insufficient time for full audit completion.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion is a serious red flag. It signals either significant weaknesses in the council's financial control environment or inability to close accounts in a timely manner. Lenders require confidence in financial statement reliability.
findings.figures: Statutory deadline 30 June 2025; audit report issued 25 February 2026 (8 months later)
findings.quote: We issued our audit report on 25th February 2026. Our audit report included a disclaimer of opinion. This means our audit report did not express an opinion on the financial statements and no assurance was provided. It was necessary to issue a disclaimer of opinion as amendments to the Account and Audit regulations introduced a statutory deadline for the publication of the Council's financial statements. We were unable to complete the audit procedures necessary to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence on which to base our opinion before the date the Council published its audited financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: The council is borrowing above its prudent liability benchmark and expects to remain so in the short term, indicating tighter funding positions than the standard risk model would suggest.
findings.detail: The liability benchmark—the minimum prudent level of borrowing a council should hold—is forecast at £115.1m for 2026/27, but the council's actual debt (excluding PFI and leases) is projected at £125.1m, exceeding the benchmark by £10m. By 2028/29, debt of £169.4m will exceed the benchmark of £159.4m by £10m. The council explicitly acknowledges this is expected and driven by planned capital expenditure.
findings.matters: Borrowing above the prudent benchmark signals the council is operating outside the standard risk parameters set by the Prudential Code, indicating financial tightness. A lender uses this as a measure of financial stress and reduced margin for error.
findings.figures: Debt 2026/27: £125.1m vs Liability Benchmark £115.1m (£10.0m above); Debt 2028/29: £169.4m vs Benchmark £159.4m (£10.0m above)
findings.quote: The table shows that the Authority expects to remain borrowed above its liability benchmark in the short term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Revenue financing costs will rise to 8.5% of the council's net revenue stream by 2028/29, driven by rising interest payable and a 75% fall in investment income.
findings.detail: Investment income is forecast to fall from £5.9m in 2024/25 to £1.5m in 2026/27 (75% reduction), while interest payable on borrowing rises from £11.3m to £13.8m over the same period. Total financing costs (interest, MRP, and investment income) will grow from 7.3% to 8.5% of net revenue funding by 2028/29. This structurally reduces budget flexibility for services.
findings.matters: A lender monitors whether the council's revenue budget has adequate headroom to absorb unexpected costs or income shortfalls. Rising financing costs as a share of budget indicate tightening financial flexibility and reduced capacity to manage demand pressures.
findings.figures: Investment income: £5.9m (2024/25) to £1.5m (2026/27); interest payable: £11.3m to £13.8m (2026-2029); total financing costs: 7.3% of net revenue stream (2026/27) rising to 8.5% (2028/29)
findings.quote: Table 11: Investment Income (interest receivable) (5.9) [2024/25] ... (1.5) [2026/27]; Interest payable 11.8 [2024/25] ... 13.8 [2028/29]

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Treasury investment balances will fall from £90.5 million to £20.0 million by 2026/27, a 78% reduction that constrains liquidity and signals heavy consumption of working capital.
findings.detail: The council's cash reserves held in treasury investments are forecast to decline steeply, from £90.5m in 2024/25 to £60.0m in 2025/26 and down to £20.0m in 2026/27 and beyond. This reflects capital spending outpacing capital receipts and grant income, forcing reliance on investment drawdown. Alongside this, the council is borrowing £49m, indicating simultaneous depletion of reserves and increase in debt.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council has sufficient liquid resources and financial flexibility to manage unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls. A rapid 78% reduction in investment balances signals reduced financial cushion and dependency on continued access to borrowing.
findings.figures: Short-term investments: £90.5m (2024/25), £60.0m (2025/26), £20.0m (2026/27-2028/29); reduction of £70.5m or 78% over two years
findings.quote: Table 9: Short-Term Investments 90.5 [2024/25 actual] ... 20.0 [2026/27 budget]

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Capital Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: The council will borrow £49 million for the 2026/27 capital programme, increasing the Capital Financing Requirement by £37.3 million.
findings.detail: Capital expenditure of £106.3m in 2026/27 will be financed 46% by new debt (£49.0m), 44% by external grants, and 8% by own resources. This new borrowing adds to the council's cumulative debt, with the Capital Financing Requirement (excluding leases) rising from £272.7m to £310.0m, and increasing further to £331.7m including accounting leases.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the scale and trajectory of council borrowing and whether debt levels remain manageable within statutory limits and the council's revenue budget.
findings.figures: £49.0m new debt in 2026/27; CFR increase of £37.3m; total CFR (including leases) forecast to reach £331.7m by 2026/27 against an authorised limit of £364.7m
findings.quote: the CFR (excluding leases) is expected to increase by £37.3 million during 2026/27... the Council's estimated CFR is as follows: General Fund services 223.3 [£m]

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Property portfolio returning 3.88% forecast for 2027 while £34.6m funded by borrowing
findings.detail: The council's commercial property investments are forecast to return 3.88% net of all costs in 2027 (rental income less borrowing interest, minimum revenue provision, and running costs). However, £34.6m of this portfolio is funded by borrowing. The council accepts these low returns because properties are held primarily for regeneration and local economy objectives rather than profit generation.
findings.matters: Borrowing to fund investments returning below typical borrowing costs requires the council to subsidize these assets from revenue, reducing financial flexibility and limiting resources available for service delivery and debt service if pressures emerge.
findings.figures: 2027 forecast return 3.88%; borrowing-funded property £34.6m (down from £37.0m in 2025)
findings.quote: The Council invests in local commercial property with the dual purpose of supporting the local economy and generating rental income to support expenditure spent on local public services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council acquired sole control of Thwaites Brewery regeneration site in 2024/25
findings.detail: The council previously held a 49% stake in a joint venture with Maple Grove Developments for the former Thwaites Brewery site in Blackburn town center. During 2024/25, it acquired Maple Grove's share of the £2.7m shareholder loans, making the council the wholly-owned controller of the site and ending private sector partnership risk-sharing.
findings.matters: Sole ownership of major regeneration projects removes the benefit of private sector involvement and shared risk. Lenders would assess the council's capacity to deliver large development projects independently without continued private sector partnership.
findings.figures: Original joint venture £2.7m total; council stake £1.323m; council now 100% owner
findings.quote: During financial year 2024/25, the Council acquired Maple Grove Developments' share in the joint venture company which is now a wholly owned entity by the Council (and thereby giving it full control of the former Thwaites site).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Sundry Commercial and Retail property showing significant cumulative losses
findings.detail: The council's commercial property portfolio is underperforming across multiple categories. Sundry Commercial Property (£13.0m purchase) carries £4.3m cumulative losses (valued £9.5m). Sundry Shops (£2.6m purchase) carries £3.7m cumulative losses (valued £2.9m). These write-downs indicate sustained market challenges in both secondary commercial and retail real estate.
findings.matters: Ongoing losses on multiple property categories suggest the portfolio is not delivering expected returns and may require further value adjustments, weakening the council's balance sheet.
findings.figures: Sundry Commercial: £13.0m purchase / £4.3m loss; Shops: £2.6m purchase / £3.7m loss
findings.quote: Sundry Commercial Property 13.0 (4.3) 9.5  Sundry Shops 2.6 (3.7) 2.9

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Residential Development Sites portfolio valued at £2.6m despite £14.4m original purchase cost
findings.detail: The council holds residential development sites acquired to support housing provision and regeneration. These sites were originally purchased for £14.4m and are now valued in the accounts at £2.6m, representing an 82% reduction from purchase cost. The 2025 annual movement shows a further £0.6m loss.
findings.matters: A major write-down on capital-committed residential development assets raises questions about the council's capacity to deliver housing regeneration projects and whether further impairment is likely.
findings.figures: Purchase cost £14.4m; current value £2.6m; 2025 loss £0.6m
findings.quote: Residential Development Sites 14.4 (0.6) 2.6

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-29
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation decision expected summer 2026 creates uncertainty for medium-term planning; £3.3m reserve set aside for LGR costs
findings.detail: Lancashire is undergoing Local Government Reorganisation with five proposals submitted to government in November 2025. Statutory consultation runs from 5 February 2026 for 7 weeks; decision expected summer 2026, with vesting day for new unitary councils set for 1 April 2028. The council has set aside £3.3m in reserves to cover its equitable share of reorganisation costs over the next two years. Budget and medium-term planning is based on the council continuing in its current form past the intended vesting day.
findings.matters: A major restructuring with vesting date 1 April 2028 creates planning uncertainty for the council and for lenders assessing medium-term sustainability. If reorganisation proceeds, the council's financial position and sustainability post-vesting is unclear. The £3.3m reserve commitment signals material costs associated with transition.
findings.figures: £3.3m set aside in reserves for LGR costs to be drawn down over next 2 years; vesting day 1 April 2028
findings.quote: the Council has taken steps to set aside resources to contribute an equitable share towards the costs of LGR in the County. Therefore £3.3m has been set aside in reserves, to be drawn down as required over the next 2 years.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-29
findings.headline: Recovery Grant Uplift of £2.317m ringfenced for DSG deficits, not available for general budget pressures
findings.detail: The council received an unexpected Recovery Grant Uplift of £2.317m in the final settlement (an improvement on the provisional settlement), targeted at upper tier councils with less than 17% funding increase over three years. The council has decided to set this aside in a Shadow DSG Reserve specifically to fund the residual High Needs DSG deficit after government support (up to 90%) expires. This means the apparent funding gain does not translate to additional service capacity or budget flexibility.
findings.matters: The uplift improves Core Spending Power but is ringfenced for a known liability. It does not add to the council's discretionary resources and suggests the council is already planning for the DSG deficit cliff after the statutory override ends in 2028.
findings.figures: £2.317m Recovery Grant Uplift in 2026/27; set aside in DSG Shadow Reserve to meet residual High Needs deficits accrued up to 31 March 2028
findings.quote: In light of this, the Council proposes to set aside the additional £2.317m of Recovery Grant Uplift funding received in the final Settlement in a DSG Shadow Reserve, to be utilised in meeting the cost of the High Needs DSG deficits accrued up to 31 st March 2028, not funded by Central Government.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-29
findings.headline: Medium-term budget gap of £5.6m by 2028/29 unresolved; Financial Strategy refresh deferred until clarity on Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: Despite a balanced budget for 2026/27, the council faces a structural gap of c£5.6m by 2028/29. The Financial Strategy (which normally set out how to bridge such gaps) was due for refresh but has been deferred pending the outcome of Local Government Reorganisation consultation and government decision expected Summer 2026. The strategy refresh is now scheduled for 2026/27.
findings.matters: The council has no current plan to address a material structural deficit within the medium term, and strategic planning is on hold pending an external reorganisation decision expected in summer 2026. If LGR proceeds, the vesting day is 1 April 2028 - just before the worst of the projected pressure.
findings.figures: £5.6m budget gap projected 2028/29
findings.quote: the Medium Term Financial Plan has been prepared on the basis of continuing in its current form, past the intended vesting day for the new unitary Councils across Lancashire of 1st April 2028. With the pending decision on Local Government Reorganisation in Lancashire expected over the Summer of 2026, the update to the Strategy will be deferred until 2026/27, when there will be greater clarity about the structure of Local Government.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-29
findings.headline: Adult Social Care budget exceeding government's notional allocation by unspecified amount
findings.detail: The council's Adult Social Care budgets will exceed the government's notional allocation for 2026/27. Government assumes adult care spend of £89.9m; the council's actual budget is higher. This suggests spending above the formula expectation, though the specific overage is not quantified in this paper.
findings.matters: The government notional allocation is the politically acceptable spend level. Budgeting above it signals the council does not believe it can meet demand within that envelope and is preparing to underfund other services or accept deficit.
findings.figures: Notional allocation £89.9m for 2026/27; actual budget exceeds this
findings.quote: The budget detailed within this report would result in the relevant Adult Social Care budgets exceeding the notional allocation for 2026/27 set out above.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-29
findings.headline: Children's social care permanence budget overspent by £9.2m in 2025/26 despite investment of £11.2m in 2026/27
findings.detail: Permanence (out of borough placements, fostering etc) is forecasting an overspend of £9.219m in 2025/26. The council is responding with additional investment of £11.2m in 2026/27, but acknowledges this remains demand-led and risky. Cost drivers are rising placement volumes and complexity of needs, though mix of placements is also suboptimal. The service is attempting to develop in-house provision but acknowledges these take time.
findings.matters: Children's social care permanence is notoriously hard to control. Rising volume and complexity of need, combined with shortfall in efficient placement mix, creates a moving target for budget control. The council's track record of overspend despite investment suggests demand is outpacing supply.
findings.figures: £9.219m permanence overspend forecast 2025/26; £11.2m additional investment in 2026/27 portfolio budget; council granted £958k grant for internal residential placement provision
findings.quote: This is due mainly to the increase in the demand for placements and the complexity of children's needs, but is also a consequence of the mix of placements being different to those assumed when the budget was constructed.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-29
findings.headline: Current year (2025/26) forecast overspend of £6.662m requiring additional draw from reserves
findings.detail: Executive Board reported in February 2026 that the council is forecasting an overspend of £6.662m in the current financial year, driven primarily by Children's and Adult Social Care demand pressures. This additional cost will have to be met from reserves, depleting the Buffer Support Reserve.
findings.matters: A reserve-funded overspend in the current year signals the council cannot hold its position even after budget setting and suggests underlying structural cost challenges.
findings.figures: £6.662m forecast overspend 2025/26
findings.quote: At the meeting of the Executive Board on 12th February 2026, a report on the Council's budget position for the current financial year was considered. This indicated a forecast overspend of £6.662m for the year which, if sustained, will need to be met from an additional contribution from the Council's reserves and balances to ensure a balanced budget.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-29
findings.headline: High Needs DSG deficit of £16.9m forecast by March 2027, carried unfunded under statutory override expiring in 2028
findings.detail: The council faces a High Needs Block overspend of £16.9m in 2026/27 against a funding allocation of £39.6m for £51.6m of forecast costs. No uplift in SEND funding despite rising demand. The statutory override allowing unfunded deficits expires 31 March 2028. The council is setting aside £2.317m Recovery Grant to meet part of the residual deficit in future years. Government support announced for historic deficits covers only up to 90%, leaving the council liable for the remainder.
findings.matters: This is a structural deficit that will eventually have to be funded from the general fund or reserves, eating into financial resilience once the statutory override ends. The National audit office reports EHCP numbers up 140% since 2015.
findings.figures: £16.940m estimated deficit by 31 March 2027; £51.565m estimated cost against £39.583m allocation; current DSG Reserve £1.687m; cumulative national High Needs deficit projected £6.6bn by March 2026, rising to £13.6bn by March 2028
findings.quote: the estimated cost of High Needs provision will be £51.565m compared to a funding allocation of £39.583m thereby giving rise to an estimated deficit of £16.940m by 31st March 2027

news_drafts.headline: Solar Farm development scheme cancelled: £1.035m virement removed in Q1
news_drafts.lead: Cancellation of an approved capital scheme for energy infrastructure suggests either cost overruns discovered post-approval or change in strategic priorities, relevant to understanding the council's capital planning discipline.

news_drafts.headline: Levelling Up Fund Town Centre scheme entirely removed from 2026/27 budget
news_drafts.lead: Levelling Up Fund grants are government-time-limited with conditions requiring timely spend. Complete removal from the year signals either scheme abandonment or delay that risks losing grant allocation.

news_drafts.headline: Blackburn Town Centre Star Square: £37.7m virement added then £34.3m slipped in same quarter
news_drafts.lead: A virement of this magnitude indicates emergency funding or major re-scoping. Immediate large slippage contradicts the approval decision and suggests the project faces significant obstacles or has stalled.
